SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL
Marcus - PMP Exam Study Plan (made Sun, Oct 18, 2026)

GOAL: Pass the PMP on Saturday, Nov 21, 2026 (testing center, 9:00 AM check-in). Target score: Above Target in People and Process.

EXAM OUTLINE (180 questions, 230 minutes, two 10-min breaks)
Domain I - People: 42%
 - Lead a team, support team performance, empower team members and stakeholders, train team, conflict mgmt, negotiation, mentoring, emotional intelligence, collaboration
Domain II - Process: 50%
 - Schedule, budget/cost, scope, quality, risk, procurement, integration, change control, governance, closing
Domain III - Business Environment: 8%
 - Compliance, benefits and value delivery, org change, external business environment changes

Note to self: roughly half the questions are agile or hybrid, so don't only study predictive. Read the question twice. Look for the BEST next step, not just a correct step.

WEEKLY STUDY GOALS
Week 1 (Oct 19 - Oct 25): Domain intro + People
 - Mon/Wed/Fri 6:00-7:30 AM: video course modules 1-4
 - Servant leadership, team development stages (Tuckman), conflict styles
 - Make flashcards for 40 key terms
 - Sat Oct 24: 30 practice questions on People, goal 75%+
Week 2 (Oct 26 - Nov 1): Process part 1
 - Scope, WBS, schedule (critical path, float, crashing vs fast tracking)
 - Cost mgmt: EVM formulas (CPI, SPI, EAC, ETC, TCPI) - memorize cold
 - Sun Nov 1: 40 mixed questions, review every wrong answer
Week 3 (Nov 2 - Nov 8): Process part 2
 - Risk, quality, procurement, stakeholder engagement, integration/change control
 - Agile: Scrum events, kanban, backlog refinement, velocity, burndown
 - Sat Nov 7: PRACTICE TEST 1 (full length, 180 Q, timed, 230 min)
Week 4 (Nov 9 - Nov 15): Weak areas + Business Environment
 - Review Practice Test 1 results Sun Nov 8 and Mon Nov 9 (log every miss by domain)
 - Compliance, benefits realization, org change, hybrid approaches
 - Sat Nov 14: PRACTICE TEST 2 (full length, timed), goal 80%+
Week 5 (Nov 16 - Nov 20): Final review
 - Mon Nov 16: review Test 2 misses
 - Tue-Wed: formulas sheet, ITTOs only where useful, agile terms
 - Thu Nov 19: light review only, 1 hour max
 - Fri Nov 20: rest, confirm ID, drive to test center to check parking
 - Sat Nov 21: EXAM

PRACTICE TEST DATES
 - Practice Test 1: Sat Nov 7, 2026, 8:00 AM
 - Practice Test 2: Sat Nov 14, 2026, 8:00 AM

RESOURCES
 - Exam Content Outline (PMI), PMBOK Guide 7th ed. + Agile Practice Guide
 - Online course (35 contact hours - certificate already done)
 - Question bank with about 1,200 questions
 - Study group with Dana and Priya on Thursdays 7:30 PM (video call)

RULES
 - Weekdays: 1.5 hr before work, 30 min flashcards at lunch
 - Weekends: 3 hr blocks
 - No studying after 9 PM, sleep matters
 - Ask manager about taking Fri Nov 20 as a half day
 - Exam fee already paid, rescheduling allowed up to 48 hrs before
notes:
PMP class notes - Marcus (wk 2-3)

TOPIC 1: EVM (earned value)
- PV = planned value, EV = earned value, AC = actual cost. BAC = total budget.
- CV = EV - AC (neg = over budget). SV = EV - PV (neg = behind sched).
- CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV. >1 good, <1 bad. Trick: EV always on top!!
- EAC formulas, 3 diff ones:
  * BAC/CPI -> if current variance will continue (typical)
  * AC + (BAC - EV) -> if var was atypical, one-time thing
  * AC + bottom-up ETC -> orig estimate was bad
- ETC = EAC - AC
- VAC = BAC - EAC
- TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(BAC - AC) -> eff. needed to finish on budget. If TCPI > 1 hard to hit.
- Ex from class: BAC 200k, EV 80k, AC 100k, PV 90k. CPI = .8, SPI = .89. EAC = 200/.8 = 250k. VAC = -50k. Bad.
- Instructor said they love giving a scenario + asking which formula, not just calc.

TOPIC 2: Risk mgmt
- Risk = uncertain event, + or -. Threat vs opportunity.
- Process: plan RM -> identify -> qualitative analysis -> quantitative analysis -> plan responses -> implement responses -> monitor
- Qualitative = prob x impact matrix, quick, subjective. Quant = Monte Carlo, decision trees, EMV (prob x $).
- Threat responses: avoid, mitigate, transfer (insurance, contract - doesn't remove the risk, just shifts ownership), accept, escalate
- Opportunity responses: exploit, enhance, share, accept, escalate
- Active accept = contingency reserve. Passive = do nothing
- Contingency reserve = known unknowns (in cost baseline). Mgmt reserve = unknown unknowns (NOT in baseline, needs approval)
- Residual risk = left after response. Secondary risk = NEW risk caused by response.
- Risk register = living doc, update each status mtg
- Risk owner assigned to each risk!
- Q to review: when risk actually happens and no plan -> workaround (not contingency)

Cr1tical Path Method (CPM)

- Critical path = longest path thru netwrok diagram; shortest possible project duratlon
- Float (slack) = how long activity can be delayed w/o delaying project end date
- Activities on critical path have zero f1oat
- Forward pass: ES, EF   EF = ES + Duration [unreadable]
- Backward pass: LF, LS   LS = LF - Duratlon
- Total float = LS - ES  (or LF - EF)
- Free f1oat = delay w/o delaying next activity's ES

Schedule compresslon:
  Crashing = add resources, $$ increases
  Fast tracking = do in parallel, rlsk increases

Note: can have more than 1 critlcal path -> more risk

Okay, so, um, let's get started. Welcome back everybody. Today we're going to talk about stakeholder engagement, which, uh, honestly is one of my favorite topics because it's where projects really succeed or fail. So, um, first thing. Who are stakeholders? Basically anybody who can affect your project or be affected by it. Sponsors, customers, team members, the folks in legal, the vendor, even, you know, the neighbors if you're building something. Right?

So the first step is identify stakeholders. And you do this early, um, like at the very beginning, in the charter stage, and then you keep doing it, because new people show up all the time. The main output there is the stakeholder register. It has names, roles, contact info, expectations, and their influence on the project. Okay?

Now, once you've identified them, you have to analyze them. And so there are a bunch of tools for this. The one everybody knows is the power-interest grid. So, um, you draw a box, and on one axis you've got power, or authority, and on the other you've got interest. High power, high interest, you manage closely. High power, low interest, you keep satisfied. Low power, high interest, you keep informed. And low power, low interest, you just monitor. And this will be on the exam, so please memorize those four quadrants and which action goes with which one. Okay, good.

Oh, by the way, sorry, unrelated, but did anybody watch the game last night? I stayed up way too late. My coffee today is not working at all. Anyway, back to it, ha.

So there's also the salience model, which looks at power, urgency, and legitimacy. And, um, the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix. That one is really useful. So you list your stakeholders down the side and across the top you have unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, and leading. You put a C where they are currently and a D where you want them to be. And the gap between C and D is your engagement work. Right? So if your sponsor is neutral and you need them supportive, you plan some activities to close that gap.

Now, um, communication. A lot of stakeholder trouble is actually just a communication problem. So in the plan you write down who needs what information, how often, and by which method. Push, pull, or interactive. Interactive is things like meetings and calls, and it's usually the most effective because you get feedback right away. Email is push. A shared wiki is pull. Okay?

And then, so, you also have to think about conflict. When two stakeholders want different things, the best approach, usually, is collaborate or problem-solve. Not force, not avoid. Although, um, there are times for each. On the exam, though, if you see a choice that says, bring them together to find a solution that works for everyone, that's usually the one.

One more thing, and then I'll let you go. The stakeholder engagement plan isn't something you write once and put in a drawer. You monitor it. You check whether people's engagement levels are changing and you adjust. So, uh, that's, I mean, that's the key. It's continuous.

Okay, announcements. Quiz 3, which covers stakeholders and communication, was going to be next week, but we're moving it to Thursday, November 5th, at the start of class. So you've got a little extra time. And please bring a calculator for the cost chapters after that. Alright, any questions? No? Great, see you Thursday.
